author: val
body: Eight megabytes of buffer and 262,144 line slots, which is 9 MB against the 128 MB the Option A image gives Codex. The size is set by the file this pane exists to open rather than by a round number: the boot stick carries the whole tree as one `SOURCE.SRC`, measured 2,769,366 bytes on `seed/Codex.img`, and it grows. A megabyte was the first choice here and it refused the only source file on the medium.

author: val
body: A file bigger than the buffer is REFUSED with its size on the glass rather than truncated. `gfat-read-file-bulk` sizes its own read from the directory entry and takes no capacity, so it would run off the end of a smaller destination and corrupt whatever the heap put there; the size is therefore checked before the read, not after.

author: val
body: The scan is two levels deep on purpose. A single per-byte recursion over the whole buffer pushes one frame per byte: measured 2026-08-11 against `SOURCE.SRC` at 2,769,366 bytes, that took about 64 MB of stack and double-faulted (`!EXC=08`, CR2 one page under the guard). Chunking bounds both levels at 4,096 frames for a buffer of any size, which is what the pixel loops in GopShot do for the same reason.

author: val
body: The bytes on the medium are ASCII, because the image writer converted each CCE code point out through `to-unicode` on the way in. Each one comes back through `from-unicode` to be a Codex character again. Reading them as CCE directly is the boundary bug this project has shipped more than once, and here it would render every letter as the wrong glyph.

author: val
body: A line is built only as far as it can be DRAWN. Building all of it costs the square of its length, because `acc & ch` copies the accumulator every character, and none of that work reaches the glass: the runs are clipped to the panel a moment later. The tree's longest line is 131,038 characters (`codex/test/errors/list-literal-too-large.codex`), which is about eight billion bytes of copying for one row of one frame. That file is not in today's `SOURCE.SRC`, whose longest line is 1,090, but nothing stops the next concatenation from carrying it.

author: val
body: The cost is honest and it is the price of a flat buffer: a keystroke at the top of a 2.7 MB file moves 2.7 MB. On a chapter-sized file it is nothing. A gap buffer is the standard cure and this is not one.

author: val
body: The capacity is a power of two so the wrap is a mask rather than a divide, and 4096 records at 12 bytes is 49,152 bytes against the 9 MB the buffer and the index already cost. It is allocated by `ged-init` and therefore shares the buffer's lifetime exactly: the close path reclaims both, so undo history does not outlive the session that typed it.

author: val
body: A byte offset is turned back into a row by bisecting the line index rather than walking it. The concatenated tree is 59,461 lines, and a walk is that many stacked frames on a machine whose heap and stack share one arena.

author: val
body: A definition line is two spaces, a name, then a space. The name ends at the first space, which is what `extract-def-name` does one layer up in `CodeBrowser` on a Text.

author: val
body: A trailing space is dropped because the line on the medium ends CRLF and `ged-chars` renders the CR as one. A chapter name compared with it still attached is the defect the gutter mark already paid for once.

author: val
body: Twelve is 8.3 plus the dot, which is the longest name `ged-name-83` can carry.

author: val
body: A FAT short name is eleven bytes, eight of base and three of extension, space-padded, with no dot stored. The Text comes back out of the directory entry with the dot put in, so it has to be taken apart again to write one.

author: val
body: `char-code` answers CCE, not ASCII, so every character crossing back to the medium goes through `to-unicode`. This is the boundary bug the tree has shipped more than once, and here it would write a file whose name no firmware could find.

target: section:Save, And The One Hot Backup
author: val
body: The backup costs no data movement, because a FAT directory entry is only a name, a first cluster and a size. The old content is not copied to `NAME.BAK`; `NAME.BAK` is pointed AT it, and the new content is written to a fresh chain under `NAME`. The previous backup's chain is released first, which is what makes it one generation.

author: val
body: THE WINDOW, stated because it is real: between the backup entry landing and the new write completing, `NAME` and `NAME.BAK` name the SAME chain. A power loss there costs no data -- both names read the old content -- but a later delete of one would free clusters the other still uses. Closing it needs a rename, which this FAT writer does not have.

author: val
body: Measured 2026-08-19: of a 59 s save of 2,896,050 bytes, the write is 57 s and every other phase is under a second, so a bar driven from the write is driven from essentially the whole wait.

author: val
body: Set-1 make codes, the same table every other pane reads: 72 up, 80 down, 75 left, 77 right, 73 page up, 81 page down, 71 home, 79 end, 28 enter, 1 escape, 88 F12.

author: val
body: The stamp is seconds since midnight off the CMOS RTC, not a wall date. It orders the annotations written in one session, which is what a reader of the bubble needs, and it does not pretend to a precision this pane can reach. Read under the update-in-progress guard, because the three registers are three separate port reads and the clock can tick between them.
